title: Teaching-GenAI
text: Course overview

title: Teaching-GenAI
text:
Who this course is for
The starting point is a statistician who is comfortable with probability, inference, linear algebra, optimization, and statistical machine learning, but is new to modern generative AI and agent systems. Prior knowledge of deep learning, Python, or agent frameworks is not assumed. Python is introduced as we need it.
This is a self-paced Topic Course for independent study. It has no fixed semester, enrollment, examinations, or grading. The course language is English, with standard terminology that can be reused in teaching and research.

title: Teaching-GenAI
text:
The learning path


01 · Understand the model
Move from likelihood and feature maps to tokens, embeddings, attention, and transformers.


02 · Understand generation
Study conditional sampling, latent variables, diffusion, adaptation, and retrieval.


03 · Understand the system
Evaluate uncertainty, build tool-using agents, and design reproducible experiments.

title: Teaching-GenAI
text:
Start here

Read the course outline: 14 ordered modules with learning goals, statistical connections, and Python practice.
Keep the statistical lens nearby as a translation guide.
Set up Python + Quarto, then run the first Python lab.
Use the reading guide for selected book sections, official tutorials, and foundational papers.

title: Teaching-GenAI
section: What I want to be able to do
text:
What I want to be able to do

Explain an LLM as a conditional probability model, including its training objective and sampling procedure.
Derive and implement a small attention mechanism, and explain how it fits inside a transformer.
Compare autoregressive, latent-variable, and diffusion approaches to generation.
Distinguish prompting, retrieval, fine-tuning, and preference optimization by what each changes.
Build a small agent that calls tools, observes results, and knows when to stop.
Evaluate a GenAI system using explicit targets, held-out tasks, baselines, uncertainty estimates, and error analysis.

title: Teaching-GenAI
text:
How we will learn
Each module follows the same sequence: a concrete question → a statistical formulation → a small Python experiment → an explanation in plain language. NumPy makes the mathematics visible; PyTorch is introduced for automatic differentiation and neural networks. Small examples come before large pretrained models.






NoteCurrent course materials



The outline, statistical connections, Python authoring guide, reading list, and first executable lab are available. The 14 modules describe the planned learning sequence; complete lecture notes and additional labs will be developed progressively.

title: Course outline
text:
Road map
Topic Course: Generative AI through the lens of statisticians
This sequence assumes a strong statistics background and begins at an introductory level in deep learning and GenAI. Modules are learning units, not calendar weeks. Work through them at a comfortable pace, returning to the mathematics when it clarifies an experiment. All proposed implementations use Python, progressing from NumPy to PyTorch and then selected pretrained-model tools.

title: Course outline
section: Part I · From statistical learning to attention
text:
Part I · From statistical learning to attention

1 · Generative AI as probabilistic modeling
Question. What does a generative model learn, and what does it mean to generate a new observation?

Learn: distinguish joint, conditional, and discriminative models; use the chain rule to factor a text distribution; connect cross-entropy to negative log likelihood.
Statistical lens: density estimation, empirical risk, smoothing, and held-out log loss.
Python practice: estimate a tiny categorical or bigram model, sample sequences, and compare training and held-out loss. The first lab starts with the categorical case.
Self-check: explain why fluent sampled text need not be factually correct, and why zero-probability events cause problems for log loss.



2 · Python and neural network foundations
Question. What changes when a regression model learns its own nonlinear features?

Learn: arrays, shapes, indexing, broadcasting, functions, and reproducible random generators; then tensors, automatic differentiation, minibatches, and a PyTorch training loop.
Statistical lens: linear/logistic regression, basis expansions, regularization, optimization, overfitting, and validation.
Python practice: fit logistic regression and a small multilayer perceptron to the same simulated problem; record train/validation curves and compare against a simple baseline.
Self-check: distinguish the model, loss, optimizer, and data split; check a derivative numerically before trusting autodiff.



3 · Tokens, embeddings, and representations
Question. How does text become something a numerical model can use?

Learn: tokenization, vocabulary, one-hot representations, embedding lookup, positional information, cosine similarity, and contextual representations.
Statistical lens: design matrices, learned feature maps, matrix factorization, and identifiability.
Python practice: tokenize a small public text collection and compare bag-of-words with embedding-based similarity. Inspect examples where similarity is misleading.
Self-check: explain why a token is not necessarily a word and why a two-dimensional embedding plot is not evidence of causal structure.



4 · Attention from first principles
Question. How can a representation select and combine information relevant to a query?

Learn: queries, keys, values, scaled dot products, row-wise softmax, self-attention, cross-attention, causal masks, and multiple heads.
Statistical lens: a query-dependent normalized weighted average; compare with kernel smoothing without claiming exact equivalence.
Python practice: calculate a three-token attention example by hand, implement it in NumPy, verify dimensions and row sums, and plot how weights change when keys change.
Self-check: explain the role of the mask and the \(\sqrt{d_k}\) scaling; describe why attention weights alone are not a faithful explanation of a prediction.
Reading: Attention Is All You Need, especially the architecture and attention equations.

title: Course outline
section: Part II · Transformers and generative models
text:
Part II · Transformers and generative models

5 · Assembling the transformer
Question. How does one attention calculation become a sequence model?

Learn: residual connections, normalization, feed-forward layers, positional encodings, encoder/decoder distinctions, and a decoder-only forward pass.
Statistical lens: a composition of fitted feature transformations with shared parameters and a conditional prediction head.
Python practice: implement a tiny decoder block in PyTorch; track every tensor’s dimensions and use a causal-mask check to show future tokens cannot influence earlier outputs.
Self-check: draw the route from token IDs to next-token probabilities, and distinguish the original encoder-decoder transformer from a decoder-only language model.



6 · Language model training, prompting, and decoding
Question. What is learned in the weights, and what changes when we provide a prompt?

Learn: next-token prediction, teacher forcing, context windows, pretraining versus inference, in-context examples, greedy decoding, temperature, top-k, and top-p.
Statistical lens: conditional likelihood, distribution shift, and transformations of a sampling distribution. In-context behavior can be studied statistically without assuming the model performs exact Bayesian inference.
Python practice: train a very small character model or use a small pretrained model; vary one decoding choice at a time on fixed prompts and repeat runs.
Self-check: explain why perplexity is not a universal measure of usefulness and why prompting is not parameter estimation by gradient descent at inference time.



7 · Latent variables, VAEs, GANs, and flows
Question. What alternatives to sequential factorization can represent a complex distribution?

Learn: the encoder/decoder view of a VAE, the evidence lower bound (ELBO), reparameterization, and a conceptual comparison with adversarial learning and invertible flows.
Statistical lens: latent-variable models, variational inference, density-ratio ideas, and change of variables. Compare objectives, sampling, and access to likelihoods.
Python practice: derive the ELBO and implement a small VAE on synthetic two-dimensional data. Treat GANs and flows as comparison topics on the first pass.
Self-check: separate the latent prior, approximate posterior, and observation model; explain why matching a few summary statistics cannot establish distributional equivalence.
Reading: Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes.



8 · Diffusion and score-based generation
Question. How can learning to remove noise support generation from noise?

Learn: a forward noising process, learned reverse transitions, denoising objectives, score functions, and conditional generation; preview image and multimodal applications.
Statistical lens: stochastic processes, denoising estimation, and the score \(\nabla_x\log p(x)\), which differs from a likelihood score with respect to model parameters.
Python practice: simulate progressive Gaussian noising on a mixture distribution, then study a small learned denoiser and the effect of the noise schedule.
Self-check: distinguish the known forward process from the fitted reverse process and separate training from sampling.
Reading: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models. Continuous-time formulations are an optional extension.



9 · Fine-tuning, LoRA, and preference learning
Question. How do we adapt an existing model, and whose preferences are represented?

Learn: supervised fine-tuning, parameter-efficient updates, LoRA, instruction data, preference data, the RLHF pipeline, and the basic DPO idea.
Statistical lens: transfer learning, regularization, low-rank parameter updates, and Bradley–Terry-style paired comparisons. Keep model quality separate from preference-label quality.
Python practice: fit a toy paired-comparison model and compare a full matrix update with a low-rank update. Small-model fine-tuning is optional after the conceptual exercise.
Self-check: explain what changes under prompting, RAG, and fine-tuning; identify label noise and selection bias in preference data.
Readings: LoRA and DPO.

title: Course outline
section: Part III · Reliable systems and agents
text:
Part III · Reliable systems and agents

10 · Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
Question. How can a model answer using a specified collection of documents?

Learn: document chunking, indexing, retrieval, reranking, context assembly, citation, and abstention when evidence is insufficient.
Statistical lens: prediction conditional on selected evidence, retrieval error, measurement error, and the interaction between pipeline components.
Python practice: build a small pipeline over public statistical notes. Inspect retrieved passages, compare with a keyword baseline, and test answerable and unanswerable questions separately.
Self-check: identify whether an error arose in retrieval, evidence selection, or generation. A citation does not by itself show that its source supports the claim.
Reading: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks.



11 · Evaluation, calibration, and uncertainty
Question. What evidence would justify saying one system is better than another?

Learn: task-specific metrics, held-out evaluation, data contamination, human annotation, LLM-as-a-judge limitations, calibration, abstention, and an introduction to conformal methods.
Statistical lens: estimands, sampling units, paired comparisons, bootstrap uncertainty, clustered dependence, and distribution shift. Conformal coverage needs an explicit target and assumptions such as exchangeability; it is not an automatic guarantee of free-text truthfulness.
Python practice: compare two fixed systems on the same held-out questions; bootstrap at the question level, inspect judge disagreement, and draw a risk-versus-coverage curve for abstention.
Self-check: distinguish token probabilities, answer confidence, and factual correctness; state the population to which a reported interval applies.
Reading: A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction.



12 · Agents: tools, state, and decisions
Question. What makes a system an agent, beyond producing a text response?

Learn: a model–action–observation loop, tool schemas, state, memory, structured outputs, retries, and stopping rules; distinguish a fixed workflow from adaptive action selection.
Statistical lens: sequential decision making, partial observation, expected utility, and the value of information. Learn the basic state/action/reward vocabulary without requiring a reinforcement learning course first.
Python practice: build a single agent with two narrow tools, such as a calculator and document lookup. Validate arguments, log actions and observations, and enforce a small step budget.
Self-check: explain when a fixed Python function or workflow is sufficient and why tool access does not imply reliable tool use.
Reading: ReAct; study observable actions and results without treating generated reasoning text as a faithful record of internal computation.



13 · Agent reliability and experimental design
Question. Does an agent improve outcomes enough to justify its additional complexity?

Learn: trajectory-level evaluation, failure taxonomies, repeated trials, cost/latency tradeoffs, memory ablations, prompt injection through retrieved text, and human approval for consequential actions.
Statistical lens: dependence within a task trajectory, factorial comparisons, uncertainty in success rates, and adaptive selection bias.
Python practice: compare a direct model call, a fixed workflow, and the agent on the same task set and budget. Inject harmless tool failures; log recovery, loop counts, and stopping behavior. Treat external documents as data rather than tool instructions.
Self-check: separate task failure, tool failure, unsupported answers, and budget exhaustion. Add multiple agents only as an optional ablation after establishing a single-agent baseline.



14 · Capstone: a GenAI system for a statistician
Choose one modest project: a citation-grounded assistant for public statistical notes, a teaching assistant that explains simulation results, or a tool-using simulation planner with a constrained action space.
Produce a reproducible Python notebook and a short Quarto chapter containing:

A target user, task population, loss, and explicit scope.
A simple baseline and one justified extension, such as RAG or tool use.
Separate development and held-out evaluation sets, with provenance.
Repeated-run results, task-level uncertainty, cost, and failure examples.
An ablation that tests what the added component contributes.
A plain-language explanation of what the evidence supports and where the system fails.

Success means being able to explain, implement, evaluate, and teach the system. A small, well-understood experiment is a complete capstone.

title: Course outline
text:
Optional directions after the core
Multimodal models, advanced diffusion/SDE theory, scaling laws, interpretability, reasoning-model training, causal questions about evaluation, and multi-agent systems can each become a later topic. Select them to answer a concrete research question rather than trying to learn every framework at once.

title: The statistical lens
text:
A translation guide
For each new idea, ask: What are the observations? What is random? What is the target? What is being optimized? What assumptions justify the evaluation? The connections below are learning aids; their limits matter as much as their similarities.

title: The statistical lens
text:
GenAI concept
Statistical starting point
What needs care




Language modeling
Conditional density estimation and the chain rule
Token likelihood measures text prediction, not the truth of a claim.


Cross-entropy training
Maximum likelihood and empirical risk minimization
Token observations within documents are dependent; split and evaluate at an appropriate unit.


Embeddings
Learned feature maps and low-dimensional representations
Coordinates are learned representations, not uniquely identified scientific factors.


Attention
Query-dependent weighted averages, reminiscent of kernel smoothing
Queries, keys, and values are learned; attention weights are not automatically causal importance or posterior probabilities.


Transformer
A composition of learned feature transformations
Attention is one component alongside positional information, nonlinear layers, and residual connections.


Temperature
A transformation of a categorical sampling distribution
More or less randomness does not by itself improve calibration or factual correctness.


Variational autoencoder
Latent-variable modeling and variational inference
The encoder approximates a posterior under the fitted model; approximation and model misspecification both matter.


Diffusion
Denoising, score estimation, and stochastic processes
A learned reverse process approximates a distribution; it does not recover a unique original observation from noise.


LoRA
A low-rank restriction on parameter updates
This is a constraint on an update matrix, not necessarily on the entire fitted model.


Preference optimization
Paired-comparison models and regularized decision making
Annotator preferences and reward proxies are not objective truth.


RAG
Retrieval followed by prediction conditional on selected evidence
Retrieved documents are selected, potentially incomplete or wrong, and usually not random samples from a posterior.


Agent
Sequential decisions with actions, observations, and a stopping rule
The language model is only one part of the system; tools, environment, and accumulated errors also matter.


LLM evaluation
Measurement, experimental design, and uncertainty quantification
Repeated answers to one prompt do not create independent test tasks.

title: The statistical lens
section: Three equations to keep in view
text:
Three equations to keep in view

A language model is a distribution over sequences
For tokens \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\),
\[
p_\theta(x_{1:T})=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}).
\]
Training commonly minimizes the sum of negative log conditional probabilities. Generation then samples from a conditional distribution, often modified by a decoding rule. Training and decoding answer different questions.


Attention forms a data-dependent weighted average
For one attention head,
\[
A=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}+M\right),
\qquad Z=AV,
\]
where softmax is applied row by row and \(M\) can mask unavailable positions. With \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n_q\times d_k}\), \(K\in\mathbb R^{n_k\times d_k}\), and \(V\in\mathbb R^{n_k\times d_v}\), the output is \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n_q\times d_v}\). Each row of \(A\) sums to one over allowed positions. This invites a comparison to a normalized smoother, while the learned representations and end-to-end training make it different from a fixed kernel estimator. See Vaswani et al..


Evaluate a system on a specified task distribution
\[
R(\pi)=\mathbb E_{\tau\sim\mathcal D}\!\left[L(\pi,\tau)\right].
\]
Here \(\pi\) is the full system, \(\tau\) a task, and \(L\) a loss that may include failure, cost, and latency. Specify the task population and sampling design before reporting a performance estimate. For stochastic systems, distinguish between-task variation from variation across repeated runs of the same task.

title: The statistical lens
section: Questions for every paper or experiment
text:
Questions for every paper or experiment

What is the estimand or target behavior, and what is actually measured?
What are the training, validation, and test units? Where could leakage enter?
Which quantities are learned, fixed, sampled, or selected adaptively?
What simple baseline would tell us whether the additional complexity helps?
How would distribution shift, dependence, or misspecification change the conclusion?
Which claims are empirically supported, and which remain useful analogies?

title: Learn and teach with Python
text:
Set up the course
Install Python and Quarto first. Python 3.12 is used for the initial verified build. In a terminal:
git clone https://github.com/chikuang/Teaching-GenAI.git
cd Teaching-GenAI
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
quarto check jupyter
quarto preview
On Windows, create the environment with py -m venv .venv and activate it in PowerShell with .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1. The remaining python and quarto commands are the same. Quarto is a separate application, so it must also be available on the terminal’s PATH.
If Quarto selects a different Python installation, set QUARTO_PYTHON to the full path of this environment’s Python executable. On macOS/Linux after activation:
export QUARTO_PYTHON="$PWD/.venv/bin/python"
Start with NumPy and Matplotlib. PyTorch and model libraries are introduced in later modules, following their current official installation instructions; they are not needed for the first lab.

We begin with a categorical distribution.

```{python}

```

title: Learn and teach with Python
text:
A repeatable lesson structure

Start with one statistical question and a small data-generating example.
Write the model, objective, and assumptions before using a high-level library.
Implement the smallest useful calculation; show shapes, outputs, and diagnostic plots.
Change one assumption or parameter and predict what should happen.
End with an explanation, a limitation, and one exercise that tests understanding.

title: First Python lab: probabilities to generation
text:
1 · Represent a probability distribution
This small experiment connects a familiar categorical model to the sampling step used in language generation. It runs on a CPU with NumPy and Matplotlib, with no model download or API account.
Download the Jupyter notebook
The web page displays results computed by Python when the course is built. To edit and run the cells yourself, open the downloaded notebook in JupyterLab or VS Code; the static web page does not run a Python kernel.
Suppose a toy model predicts the next token from a vocabulary of three words. These probabilities are supplied for illustration; we have not trained a language model.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

tokens = np.array(["statistics", "learning", "agents"])
p = np.array([0.60, 0.30, 0.10])
assert np.isclose(p.sum(), 1.0)
print(dict(zip(tokens.tolist(), p.tolist())))

{'statistics': 0.6, 'learning': 0.3, 'agents': 0.1}
np.array creates a numerical array. Python indexing starts at zero, so p[0] is the first probability. np.isclose compares floating-point values with a tolerance. assert stops execution if a check fails.
crumbs: First Python lab: probabilities to generation

title: First Python lab: probabilities to generation
text:
2 · Evaluate log loss
For observations \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\) drawn from a categorical distribution, the average negative log likelihood is
\[
\widehat L(p)=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\log p_{y_i}.
\]
Here the observations are token indices. The array p[observed] looks up the predicted probability of each observed token.

observed = np.array([0, 0, 1, 0, 2, 1])
model_loss = -np.log(p[observed]).mean()
uniform = np.full(3, 1 / 3)
uniform_loss = -np.log(uniform[observed]).mean()
print(f"Toy model log loss: {model_loss:.3f} nats per token")
print(f"Uniform log loss:   {uniform_loss:.3f} nats per token")

Toy model log loss: 1.041 nats per token
Uniform log loss:   1.099 nats per token


This tiny sample is an illustration of the calculation, not evidence that one model will outperform another on a target population. In a real comparison, choose the model on development data and evaluate on separate held-out observations. Natural logarithms give losses in nats.
crumbs: First Python lab: probabilities to generation

title: First Python lab: probabilities to generation
text:
3 · Change the sampling temperature
Given logits \(z_j\) and temperature \(T>0\), the sampling probabilities are
\[
p_T(j)=\frac{\exp(z_j/T)}{\sum_k\exp(z_k/T)}.
\]
Taking \(z_j=\log p_j\) recovers the original distribution at \(T=1\). Lower temperatures concentrate probability on higher-scoring tokens. Higher temperatures move this finite-vocabulary distribution toward uniformity. Neither operation establishes that a generated statement is true.

def softmax(logits, temperature=1.0):
    if temperature <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Temperature must be positive.")
    scaled = np.asarray(logits, dtype=float) / temperature
    weights = np.exp(scaled - scaled.max())
    return weights / weights.sum()

logits = np.log(p)
temperatures = [0.5, 1.0, 2.0]
probabilities = np.vstack([softmax(logits, t) for t in temperatures])
assert np.allclose(probabilities.sum(axis=1), 1.0)
assert np.allclose(softmax(logits, 1.0), p)
for t, row in zip(temperatures, probabilities):
    print(f"T={t:.1f}: {np.round(row, 3)}")

T=0.5: [0.783 0.196 0.022]
T=1.0: [0.6 0.3 0.1]
T=2.0: [0.473 0.334 0.193]


Subtracting the maximum before exponentiation leaves softmax unchanged and reduces overflow risk. A function is defined with def; indentation defines its body. The list comprehension computes one row for each temperature, and np.vstack combines the rows into a matrix.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(layout="constrained")
x = np.arange(len(tokens))
width = 0.24
colors = ["#203f68", "#c88a30", "#728aa5"]
for i, (t, row, color) in enumerate(zip(temperatures, probabilities, colors)):
    ax.bar(x + (i - 1) * width, row, width, label=f"T = {t}", color=color)
ax.set_xticks(x, tokens)
ax.set_ylabel("Sampling probability")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(title="Temperature", frameon=False)
plt.show()







Figure 1: Temperature changes the sampling distribution of the toy model.
crumbs: First Python lab: probabilities to generation

title: First Python lab: probabilities to generation
section: 4 · Generate and inspect a Monte Carlo sample
text:
4 · Generate and inspect a Monte Carlo sample

rng = np.random.default_rng(8670)
draws = rng.choice(len(tokens), size=10_000, p=softmax(logits, 1.0))
frequencies = np.bincount(draws, minlength=len(tokens)) / len(draws)
print("Target:   ", p)
print("Observed: ", np.round(frequencies, 3))
print("One draw: ", tokens[draws[0]])

Target:    [0.6 0.3 0.1]
Observed:  [0.592 0.303 0.105]
One draw:  statistics


A fixed seed makes this example reproducible within the recorded environment. Sampling variation remains part of the statistical experiment. These independent draws are a toy example; an autoregressive language model instead updates its conditional distribution after each generated token.
crumbs: First Python lab: probabilities to generation

title: First Python lab: probabilities to generation
text:
Try it yourself

Change p while preserving positivity and a sum of one. Predict the temperature effect before running the code.
Repeat the Monte Carlo experiment with smaller sample sizes. Compare observed variability with the multinomial variance formula.
Try two different candidate distributions on the same observations. Explain why the lower observed loss alone is not a generalization guarantee.
Replace sampling by choosing the highest-probability token. Which aspect of the distribution disappears?
crumbs: First Python lab: probabilities to generation

title: First Python lab: probabilities to generation
text:
Bridge to attention
Softmax will return in attention, where it normalizes similarity scores into weights over available positions. The normalization is the same mathematical operation, but its role differs: attention weights combine value vectors, whereas the probabilities above sample an output token. The statistical lens introduces the attention equation.

Foundational papers by module

Attention and transformers — Module 4–5: Vaswani et al. (2017), Attention Is All You Need. First identify the inputs, outputs, attention equation, and block diagram; return to experiments later.
Latent-variable generation — Module 7: Kingma and Welling (2013 preprint), Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes. Connect the ELBO to variational inference and study the reparameterization step.
Diffusion — Module 8: Ho, Jain, and Abbeel (2020), Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models. Track the forward and reverse processes and the denoising objective.
Efficient adaptation — Module 9: Hu et al. (2021 preprint), LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. Identify which parameters are frozen and which low-rank matrices are learned.
Preference learning — Module 9: Rafailov et al. (2023), Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model. Study the preference likelihood and the role of the reference policy.
Retrieval — Module 10: Lewis et al. (2020), Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks. Identify the retriever, generator, and conditioning information; distinguish the original model from a simple modern retrieval pipeline.
Uncertainty — Module 11: Angelopoulos and Bates (2021 preprint), A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification. Establish the prediction target, calibration set, and coverage assumptions before applying the ideas to generated outputs.
Agents — Module 12: Yao et al. (2022 preprint; ICLR 2023), ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models. Follow the interaction with tools and observations, and inspect how success is measured.

title: Reading guide
text:
A statistician’s reading note
For each paper, write a short note answering: What is the statistical object? What is optimized? What assumptions are made? What is the comparison baseline? What are the experimental units? Which claim would I want to reproduce?
Links and source identities were checked when this outline was created on October 20, 2026. Software documentation evolves; record the versions used for each future lab.
